questions.question: Discuss on reinforcements used in plastics and their advantages. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss on reinforcements used in plastics and their advantages. [U]/ [CO3]
  • Reinforcements used in plastics include materials such as glass fibres, carbon fibres, asbestos, and
  • synthetic fibres, which are incorporated into polymer matrices to improve their performance.
  • During processing, these reinforcements play an important role by increasing the strength of the
  • material without causing a significant increase in weight, thus maintaining a high strength -to-
  • weight ratio. In the final product, they enhance key mechanical properties such as tensile strength,
  • stiffness, and impact resistance, making the material more durable and reliable. The advantages of
  • using reinforcements in plastics include improved mechanical strength, better dimensional
  • stability, increased resistance to wear and deformation, and suitability for demanding applications
  • in fields like automotive, aerospace, and construction. (Explanation 2 marks Advantages 2 marks)

• List any four properties of elastomers. [K]/ [CO4]

  • structure. They can undergo large reversible deformations, meaning they can be stretched
  • significantly and return to their original shape when the stress is removed. Elastomers generally

  • and wear. Additionally, elastomers show good chemical resistance and can withstand a wide range
  • of temperatures, making them suitable for applications such as rubber products, seals, and gaskets.

questions.question: Outline emulsion polymerization with its components. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Outline emulsion polymerization with its components. [An]/ [CO4]
  • Emulsion polymerization is a type of free radical polymerization carried out in an aqueous medium
  • where the monomer is emulsified in water with the help of surfactants. In this process, the
  • monomer forms small droplets stabilized by an emulsifying agent, a nd polymerization occurs
  • mainly within micelles formed by the surfactant. A water -soluble initiator, such as potassium
  • persulfate, decomposes to produce free radicals, which enter the micelles and initiate
  • polymerization, leading to the formation of polymer particles dispersed in water (latex).
  • The main components of emulsion polymerization include: (1) Monomer, which is the substance
  • to be polymerized (e.g., styrene, butadiene); (2) Water, acting as the dispersion medium; (3)
  • Emulsifier or surfactant, which stabilizes the monomer droplets and fo rms micelles; (4) Initiator,
  • usually water-soluble (e.g., persulfates), which generates free radicals; and sometimes (5) Buffer
  • or stabilizers, to maintain pH and stability of the system. The advantages of this method include
  • better heat control, high polymerization rate, and production of high molecular weight polymers,
  • making it widely used in the manufacture of synthetic rubber, paints, and adhesives.
  • (Method- 4 marks components – 3marks)

questions.question: Explain the manufacture of nitro benzene with reaction. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the manufacture of nitro benzene with reaction. [U]/[CO1]
  • Nitrobenzene is manufactured by the nitration of benzene using a nitrating mixture of concentrated
  • nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid. In this process, benzene is treated with the acid mixture
  • at about 50 –60°C. Sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst and dehydrating agent, generating the active
  • nitrating species, the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺), from nitric acid. This nitronium ion then attacks the
  • benzene ring in an electrophilic substitution reaction, replacing one hydrogen atom to form
  • nitrobenzene.
  • The reaction is represented as: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O (in presence of conc. H₂SO₄)
  • After the reaction, the mixture is allowed to settle, and nitrobenzene is separated, washed, and
  • purified. This method is widely used in industry for the large -scale production of nitrobenzene,
  • which is an important intermediate in the manufacture of anili ne, dyes, and pharmaceuticals.
  • (Method 5 marks equation 2 marks)

questions.question: Explain the properties and applications of thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the properties and applications of thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.
  • [U]/[CO3]
  • Thermoplastics are linear or slightly branched polymers that soften on heating and harden on
  • cooling, and this process is reversible. They possess properties such as flexibility, low to moderate
  • strength, ease of moulding, recyclability, and good chemical resistance. Common examples
  • include polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Thermoplastics are
  • widely used in applications such as packaging materials, plastic containers, pipes, electrical
  • insulation, and household items due to their ease of processing and reusability.
  • In contrast, thermosetting plastics are highly cross -linked polymers that undergo a permanent
  • chemical change when heated and cannot be remelted or reshaped. They are hard, rigid, and brittle
  • with high thermal stability, excellent mechanical strength, and good resistance to chemicals and
  • deformation. Examples include bakelite, urea-formaldehyde, and epoxy resins. These plastics are
  • used in applications requiring durability and heat resistance, such as electrical fittings, adhesives,
  • laminates, coatings, and automotive parts. Thus, thermoplastics are preferred for recyclable and
  • flexible applications, whereas thermosetting plastics are suitable for high -strength and heat -
  • resistant uses. (Any 3 points from each type with one example give full credit)

questions.question: Explain the preparation of nylon-6,6 using hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid with a neat reaction. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the preparation of nylon-6,6 using hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid with a
  • neat reaction. [U]/[CO2]
  • Nylon-6,6 is prepared by the condensation polymerization of hexamethylene diamine and adipic
  • acid. Initially, equimolar amounts of hexamethylene diamine (H₂N –(CH₂)₆–NH₂) and adipic acid
  • (HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH) are mixed. This is then heated at about 250–280°C under pressure, during
  • which condensation occurs with the elimination of water molecules, leading to the formation of
  • long-chain polyamide known as nylon-6,6.
  • The reaction can be represented as: n H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂ + n HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH →
  • [–NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
  • This process results in a linear polymer with repeating amide ( –CONH–) linkages, which impart
  • high strength and durability. Nylon-6,6 thus produced is widely used in fibres, textiles, ropes, tyres,
  • and engineering plastics due to its excellent mechanical strength, abrasion resistance, and thermal
  • stability. (Explanation 5 marks equation 2 marks)

questions.question: Describe the advantages and applications of transfer moulding. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the advantages and applications of transfer moulding. [U]/[CO3]
  • Transfer moulding is a method used mainly for moulding thermosetting plastics, where the
  • material is first heated in a chamber and then transferred into a closed mould cavity. This process
  • offers several advantages, such as better surface finish and dimens ional accuracy compared to
  • compression moulding, as the material flows uniformly into the mould. It is suitable for moulding
  • complex shapes and intricate designs, including inserts like metal components, as it ensures proper
  • encapsulation. The process also reduces internal stresses, minimizes material wastage, and
  • provides improved mechanical properties in the final product.
  • The applications of transfer moulding are mainly found in the electrical and electronics industries
  • for manufacturing components such as switches, circuit breakers, connectors, and encapsulated
  • coils. It is also used in the production of automotive parts, appliance components, and moulded
  • items requiring high precision and good surface finish. Thus, transfer moulding is widely preferred
  • for producing high-quality, detailed thermosetting plastic products.
  • (3 points from advantages and applications give 3.5 marks)

questions.question: Using the properties of PAN, explain its suitability for fibers, filtration membranes, and protective materials. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Using the properties of PAN, explain its suitability for fibers, filtration membranes, and
  • protective materials. [U]/[CO2]
  • Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) is a synthetic polymer characterized by the presence of strong polar nitrile
  • (–CN) groups along its backbone, which impart several desirable properties. PAN exhibits high
  • tensile strength, good thermal stability, excellent chemical resistance, and resistance to sunlight
  • and weathering. It also has good fibre -forming ability due to strong intermolecular interactions
  • between nitrile groups, resulting in closely packed, crystalline structures.
  • These properties make PAN highly suitable for fibres, where it is used to produce acrylic fibres
  • that are lightweight, strong, and resistant to abrasion, with good resistance to chemicals and
  • environmental degradation. In filtration membranes, PAN’s chemic al resistance and stability,
  • along with its ability to form fine porous structures, make it effective for separating particles and
  • impurities in water and air filtration systems. For protective materials, PAN is valuable due to its
  • thermal stability and re sistance to chemicals, and it is also used as a precursor for carbon fibres,
  • which are widely used in protective clothing, aerospace components, and high-strength materials.
  • Thus, the combination of strength, stability, and chemical resistance makes PAN su itable for
  • diverse advanced applications.
  • (PAN explanation 1 mark. 2 marks each for any 2 points for the suitability for fiber, membrane
  • and protective materials.)

questions.question: Describe preparation, properties, and uses of nitroethane, 1-nitropropane and 2-nitropropane. / [CO1] [7x5 = 35]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe preparation, properties, and uses of nitroethane, 1-nitropropane and 2-nitropropane.
  • [U]/ [CO1]
  • Nitroalkanes such as nitroethane, 1-nitropropane, and 2-nitropropane are prepared by treating alkyl
  • halides with silver nitrite (AgNO₂) . C₂H₅X + AgNO₂ → C₂H₅NO₂ + AgX (nitroethane)
  • C₃H₇X + AgNO₂ → C₃H₇NO₂ + AgX (nitropropanes, giving both 1- and 2-isomers).
  • These compounds exhibit characteristic properties due to the presence of the electron -
  • withdrawing –NO₂ group. They are polar, have relatively high boiling points, and are moderately
  • soluble in water but highly soluble in organic solvents. Primary nitroalka nes (nitroethane and 1 -
  • nitropropane) show tautomerism (nitro –aci form) and are acidic in nature, whereas secondary
  • nitroalkanes (2-nitropropane) are less acidic. They undergo reactions such as reduction to amines
  • and condensation reactions.
  • In terms of uses, nitroethane is used as a solvent, fuel additive, and intermediate in organic
  • synthesis. 1-Nitropropane is used as a solvent for paints, coatings, and inks, while 2-nitropropane
  • is widely used as an industrial solvent and in the manufactur e of pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and
  • explosives. Thus, these nitroalkanes are important both as solvents and as intermediates in
  • chemical industries. (Preparation 2 marks properties 2.5 marks and uses 2.5 marks)
  • [7x5 = 35]

questions.question: Describe the manufacture of polystyrene by bulk polymerisation. Explain the preparation steps, properties, and applications of polystyrene. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the manufacture of polystyrene by bulk polymerisation. Explain the preparation steps,
  • properties, and applications of polystyrene. [A]/ [CO2]
  • Polystyrene is manufactured by bulk polymerization (mass polymerization) using styrene
  • monomer. In this method, pure styrene is taken in a reactor along with a small amount of initiator
  • such as benzoyl peroxide. The mixture is heated to about 80–150°C in the absence of solvent. The
  • initiator decomposes to form free radicals, which initiate chain polymerization of styrene. As the
  • reaction proceeds, viscosity increases and the polymer is formed. The process is carried out in
  • stages to control heat and avoid a uto-acceleration. Finally, the molten polymer is cooled and
  • solidified to obtain polystyrene.
  • The reaction can be represented as: n CH₂=CH–C₆H₅ → [–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–]ₙ
  • Preparation steps: Initially, purified styrene monomer is mixed with an initiator. The mixture is
  • heated gradually in a reactor under controlled temperature and pressure. Polymerization begins
  • with free radical formation and continues with chain propagatio n. The increasing viscosity is
  • managed by stepwise heating. After completion, the polymer is cooled, extruded, and cut into
  • granules for commercial use.
  • Properties: Polystyrene is a transparent, rigid, and lightweight thermoplastic with good
  • dimensional stability. It has excellent electrical insulating properties and is resistant to acids and
  • alkalis but is attacked by organic solvents. It is brittle in nature and has low impact strength, though
  • it can be modified (as high-impact polystyrene). It softens on heating and can be easily moulded.
  • Applications: Polystyrene is widely used in the manufacture of disposable cups, plates, and
  • packaging materials (thermocol/expanded polystyrene). It is used for electrical insulation, toys,
  • household items, laboratory ware, and as foam for thermal insulation in refrigerators and buildings.
  • Thus, due to its ease of processing, low cost, and useful properties, polystyrene has extensive
  • commercial applications. (2.5 marks each for bulk polymerisation and preparation step 5 marks
  • each for properties and applications)
